quote: Auch entsteht das Problem ein beliebiges 2n Eck, dessen Seiten in vorgeschriebener Richtung → zusammengeordnet sind und so die Summe der Winkel der- selben Cyklus $= 2\pi$ sind so zusammen zu biegen, dass eine singu- laritätenfreie regu[-...-]läre Fläche entsteht.
english: There also arises the problem of bending together an arbitrary 2n-gon, whose sides are paired in a prescribed direction and such that the sums of the angles of the same cycle are $2\pi$, so that a regular surface free of singularities results.
topic: Hilbert notes the problem of bending a 2n-gon with identified sides into a regular surface, sketches the Boy surface, Klein bottle and ring surface as polygon identifications, proposes realizing Boy's surface algebraically, asks questions about surfaces with prescribed double curves and about embedding projective space in 4-space, and begins a remark on classifying partial differential equations by their characteristic equation.

triage.modern_statement: Take a Euclidean polygon with 2n sides. Pair its sides with prescribed orientations so that the angles at each vertex cycle add up to 2π. The glued surface then carries a flat metric with no cone points. The question is whether this flat surface can be isometrically 'bent' into Euclidean 3-space as a regular surface with no singularities, either embedded or immersed. By Gauss–Bonnet, a closed flat surface has Euler characteristic 0, so the only cases are the flat torus and the flat Klein bottle. If 'bending' is read only topologically, as smoothly realizing any polygon gluing in R^3, the question becomes the classical one of embedding or immersing closed surfaces in R^3, as with Boy's surface for the projective plane. But Hilbert's angle condition points to the metric reading.
triage.answered_by: Classical results plus Nash (1954) and Kuiper (1955). A compact C^2 surface in R^3 always has a point of positive Gaussian curvature, so a flat torus has no C^2 or smooth isometric embedding. In the C^1 class, the Nash–Kuiper theorem gives isometric embeddings of flat tori. Borrelli, Jabrane, Lazarus and Thibert made such an embedding explicit and visualized it (PNAS, 2012, the 'Hevea' project). The Klein bottle part (immersion only, never embedding) is classical topology and is not covered by the sources I found.

evidence.claim: Smooth embeddings of the torus in Euclidean space cannot keep its flat metric, but a C^1 isometric embedding is possible.
Borrelli, Jabrane, Lazarus and Thibert built and visualized explicit C^1 isometric embeddings of flat tori in 3-space using convex integration, based on Nash–Kuiper.
The 2012 construction is described as an isometric embedding of the flat torus in 3D space made with convex integration.
The Nash–Kuiper C^1 isometric embedding theorem is presented together with an explicit construction for a flat torus.
Liebmann-type result: a compact surface in R^3 must have a point of positive curvature, which rules out C^2 flat closed surfaces.

triage.why: I read the angle-sum condition as defining a flat metric without cone points. By Gauss–Bonnet that leaves only the torus and the Klein bottle. With that reading the question splits cleanly. In the C^2 or smooth class it is impossible, by the classical compactness/curvature argument. In the C^1 class it is possible, by Nash–Kuiper (1954–55), made explicit in 2012. Convex integration and the h-principle for isometric embeddings are still active research areas. None of my sources links this note to Hilbert himself, and it is not one of his 23 published problems or the 24th. If he meant only a topological realization, the answer is instead classical surface topology: every closed surface can be immersed in R^3 (for example Boy's surface), but only orientable ones can be embedded. That is why my confidence is medium rather than high.
